planting.note: Direct sow after last frost; Burpee Butterbush is a compact, non-vining bush-type butternut squash bred to produce full-sized butternut fruit on a plant small enough for raised beds and container culture, unlike standard sprawling butternut vines that need 50-100 square feet.

directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills spaced 2-3 feet apart, or start indoors and transplant after the danger of frost has passed. Burpee Butterbush was bred to solve the space problem that keeps many gardeners from growing butternut squash — standard butternut vines sprawl 10-15 feet and can overrun a small garden — by combining a compact, bush-type growth habit that stays within a 3-4 foot footprint with fruit that is essentially identical in size, shape, and sweet, nutty flavor to full-sized vining butternut varieties. This makes it one of the few butternut options practical for raised beds, small gardens, and even large containers. Vines still produce a running habit to a modest degree as the season progresses, but nowhere near the sprawl of standard butternut, and yield per plant is comparable to vining types when given full sun and consistent water. Harvest when the tan rind is hard enough to resist a fingernail and the stem has begun to dry and corky, then cure in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks before storage to concentrate sugars and toughen the skin for long keeping.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Winter Squash Variety Trials

common_name: Black Futsu Squash (Japanese Heirloom Kabocha-Type Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost; Black Futsu is a Japanese heirloom squash known for deeply ribbed, warty, near-black skin that fades to a warm tan-orange as it cures in storage, with dense, sweet, chestnut-flavored flesh prized by chefs.

directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, allowing plenty of room for the vigorous, sprawling vines. Black Futsu is a Japanese heirloom squash valued for its striking appearance — small, flattened, deeply ribbed fruit covered in a warty, near-black rind when first harvested, which fades over several weeks of storage to a warm tan-orange with a slight bloom, a color transformation that also signals improving flavor and sweetness. The dense, dry, deep orange flesh has a rich, sweet, chestnut-like flavor considered among the best of any winter squash by many chefs, excellent roasted, pureed into soup, or used anywhere a rich kabocha-type squash is called for. Vines are vigorous and productive, typically setting several fruit per plant, each running 2-3 pounds, a manageable size for a single meal without excess storage bulk. Harvest when the rind resists a fingernail and the stem has dried and corked, then cure in a warm, dry spot for two to three weeks before eating — Black Futsu's flavor and sweetness improve markedly with curing and continue to develop in storage over the following months.

common_name: Sibley Squash (Pike's Peak Heirloom Winter Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost; Sibley, also known as Pike's Peak squash, is an 1880s heirloom prized for its distinctive teardrop shape, thin blue-gray rind, and exceptionally sweet, dry, fine-grained orange flesh that many heirloom growers consider among the best-flavored of all winter squash.

directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, allowing generous room for the long, vigorous vines. Sibley squash, introduced in the 1880s and also sold as Pike's Peak squash, is an American heirloom valued by generations of gardeners for its unusual teardrop or pear shape, thin, smooth, blue-gray rind, and exceptionally sweet, dry, fine-textured deep orange flesh with almost no fiber, a texture and flavor that many long-time growers rank above modern hybrid winter squash. Fruits typically run 6-10 pounds, large enough to serve a crowd, and the thin rind, while making the squash slightly more vulnerable to handling damage than thick-shelled types, also makes it easier to peel and cook than harder-shelled Hubbard-type squash. Vines are long and productive given full sun and consistent moisture during fruit set. Harvest when the rind has hardened and resists a fingernail and the stem has begun to dry, then cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry location before storing in a cool, dry spot, where well-cured fruit keeps for several months while its sweetness continues to improve.

common_name: Gete Okosomin Squash (Ancient Native American 'Get Big' Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost, giving vines ample room to sprawl; Gete Okosomin, meaning roughly 'big old squash' in Anishinaabemowin, is an ancient variety grown by the Miami and other Great Lakes Native nations, propagated from seed found in a centuries-old archaeological cache and reintroduced to cultivation by tribal seed-saving efforts.

directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, giving the vigorous, sprawling vines generous room. Gete Okosomin — an Anishinaabemowin name often translated as 'big old squash' or 'cool old squash' — is an heirloom traced to seed recovered from a centuries-old clay pot in an archaeological context associated with Native peoples of the Great Lakes region, and subsequently grown out, verified, and shared by Miami Nation seed keepers and Native seed-saving networks, making it one of the oldest documented squash varieties still in cultivation in North America. Fruits are large, often 10-15 pounds, striped in shades of green, orange, and cream on a somewhat elongated, ribbed form, with dense, deep orange, sweet flesh well suited to baking, soups, and pies. As a Cucurbita maxima type, it needs a long, warm growing season and ample space for its long vines, along with consistent moisture during flowering and fruit set to size the large fruit properly. Beyond its culinary value, growing Gete Okosomin is a way for gardeners to participate directly in the ongoing revival of an Indigenous foodway; seed saved from open-pollinated fruit can be replanted, continuing a lineage that stretches back many generations. Harvest when the rind is fully hardened and the stem has dried, then cure for two to three weeks before storing in a cool, dry location.

common_name: Queensland Blue Pumpkin (Australian Heirloom Blue-Gray Winter Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost; Queensland Blue is a classic 19th-century Australian heirloom pumpkin prized for its deeply ribbed, hard, blue-gray rind, dense sweet orange flesh, and outstanding storage life of six months or longer.

directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, allowing generous room for the vigorous vines. Queensland Blue is a classic Australian heirloom pumpkin, developed in the 19th century and still one of the most widely grown pumpkin varieties in Australia, valued for its distinctive, deeply ribbed, slate-blue-gray rind — a color that stands out dramatically against typical orange pumpkins in a fall display — and its dense, dry, sweet, deep orange flesh well suited to roasting, soups, and pies. The hard rind, while tough to cut into, is also the reason for the variety's outstanding keeping quality; well-cured fruit routinely stores for six months or longer in a cool, dry location, among the best storage life of any winter squash. Fruits typically run 8-12 pounds with a flattened, ribbed shape. Vines are vigorous and productive given full sun, fertile soil, and consistent moisture during fruit set. Harvest when the rind is fully hardened and resists a fingernail, and the stem has dried and corked, then cure in a warm, dry spot for two to three weeks before moving to cool storage, where the flavor continues to sweeten over the following months.
